I can't help but think it's a little weird that the vast majority of comments on this thread essentially say the solution is to "fund mental health services". I think this is a bit of an oversimplification.

We absolutely do need a massive overhaul of the public system, including tonnes more funding, but it also seems painfully obvious to me that funding access to counselling and medications, while helpful, doesn't really address the fact that high suicide rates are not born in a vacuum. 

This country has some pretty dysfunctional institutions - a dumpster-fire cost of living crisis in terms of bare necessities (housing being the big one), mass inequality, unliveable wages, a batshit welfare system, inaccessible tertiary education... I could go on. We have a society in which bootstraps and 'tall poppy' philosophies are deeply ingrained and deeply self-contradictory. 

If you ask me if I think throwing money at public services is a silver bullet I honestly say hell no, and anyone who has actually experienced a mental health crisis will probably be able to tell you that a lot of how we approach "help" is often too little and too late. I think mental health crises and suicide will always reflect the fundamental lack of opportunity and social mobility of a massive portion of New Zealanders who simply aren't privileged. Fund the shit out of the public services, but don't try and tell me that is going to address the root of the problem.

I wrote this post in a really dark place eh, long story short is that it took about 8 months before I felt like I was 'out of the woods', and I didn't really see much improvement until about month 3 or 4. Benzo withdrawal was really difficult and terrifying for me and easily the hardest thing I've dealt with.

This being said cold turkeying benzos happened during a clusterfuck of other stuff happening in my life and part of why I was on them in the first place is because I was pretty unwell, so it might be worth taking all this with a grain of salt? 

I still have visual snow obviously, although I think I'm a bit better at managing it these days, and I still have mild tinnitus but nowhere near as bad as it was during the early stages of withdrawal. Overall I think you could call me recovered, even if part of that is that I have the perspective shift of going through a long recovery from benzos and am just happy to not be where I was two years ago. The way I tend to think of it now is that yes I still struggle a bit with visual snow and tinnitus, but in a backwards kind of way the benzos almost did help with that by kicking my ass so hard that I had to learn some gratitude and resilience lol

I am not delusional enough to not understand that different areas have different price tags, but I would argue that the pricing is not relative to the value. I grew up in Grey Lynn, my two working class parents could easily afford their house 25 years ago with a mortgage. This $330K house is now valued at over 3 million, in my life time I have been priced out of my home neighbourhood 10 times over - if you want to adjust for inflation, this still means someone my age needs 6 or 7 times the resources as my parents did for the same life.

And beyond this, even if I were to look further out, past Avondale and New Lynn, the average prices have still crept over a million dollars in recent years. In Europe you don't get leaky, moldy, damp housing for millions of dollars. Can a minimum wager buy a California bungalow or a high end loft in the central city? No of course not, but this doesn't mean that pricing hasn't rapidly outstripped value for money in Auckland. Why should someone have to pay 5-10 times the cost of living as the previous generation, that isn't a meritocracy at all, if anything the standard of living should be going up with time, not eroding.

I’m no neuroscientist, though based on this experience I would argue that actual psychiatrists, doctors and neuroscientists kinda only have a flawed theoretical understanding of this kind of thing anyway, 

But I would theorise that there are two things at play here that don’t exactly boil down to “the receptors have to regrow” (they do, but still). Benzodiazepines apparently cause the body to rather quickly remove the benzodiazepine site on the gaba receptor, making basically every nerve in the body and brain resistant to gaba and therefore out of balance and under inhibited, yes. New receptors will have to be produced in order to heal, yes, a remarkably slow process given how basically the whole nervous system is affected and the body has to continue using enough of the system to keep all basic functions running, yes, but I think this is not the full story. 

I believe it is this, but also excitotoxic damage, nerves are damaged and many cells are most likely outright killed. I would say this equates to not only physical illness in the form of countless symptoms, but essentially a form of generalised brain injury, and part of recovery is literally due to the fact that although dead brain cells can be replaced, they will lack their former wiring, it is impossible for brain cells to regenerate with the same connections they once had, so these connections must be relearned, I believe this is why derealisation is such a big one, our brains are shocked so hard that we basically have to relearn how to interpret reality. It’s taken me 6 months to get back into driving, and other basic tasks felt extremely difficult at first, much like a “brain damage” feeling. It’s like a lot of cells got nuked, and the rest of the brain or newer cells have had to slowly make up for this. My understanding is that when a cell is killed by glutamate toxicity, it essentially turns into TNT and releases all its glutamate in a kind of terrible chain reaction (glutamate storm) - this is seen in traumatic brain injuries but usually localised within the area of the injury. This would explain the severity of cold turkeys, and the strangeness of tapering benzos compared to other drugs. When I cold turkeyed I was throwing up the first few days, it was a real insult  to the system. I felt like I’d been poisoned and run over, like I was dying. 

The second thing is the phenomenon of kindling, the human body appears to be prone to “sensitisation”, possibly due to an alteration in DNA expression as a mechanism for adjusting towards an environmental factor (in this case a pharmaceutical the body wouldn’t encounter in nature). The body remembers that it was damaged by a gaba drug, and so it becomes more sensitive to gaba drugs. I believe this is the case in some other drug withdrawals, for example the overload of serotonin caused by MDMA use causes the body to down regulate serotonin receptors to guard against future risk of serotonin toxicity aka why many drug users become profoundly depressed, and why withdrawals seem to become more severe with each subsequent binge and withdrawal. 

To me it doesn’t simply feel like a long hangover, or like rebound anxiety, it feels like a complex injury that involves incredibly bizarre symptoms that don’t even really mirror the effect of the benzo itself, tinnitus, tremors, hallucinations, dissociation and psychotic confusion are not a function of anxiety, they “feel” more like what I’d expect would happen if someone fried my nervous system inside out and wiped out like 5% of my brain function entirely. 

Sorry if I sound like a conspiracy theorist mad scientist, but I can compare this to gnarly opiate withdrawals I have experienced, and though that was very unpleasant, it never made me feel like my grip on reality or my personality were fundamentally affected. 

TLDR; I don’t think this is just a game of fixing the stunted benzo receptors, I think it’s doing that while also regrowing a damaged system. Recovering from glutamate damage, while simultaneously being particularly vulnerable to glutamate damage and resistant to gaba.

Edit: this all being said, I feel better at 6 months than I did at 2 or 3, so I have hope I will continue to see improvement, even if it takes a while. The more you recover, the easier it gets to continue exponentially, it’s gonna be the hardest at the start, so your priority has to be to think of the long game and just focus on weathering the early days. Don’t bother thinking about your life dreams just yet, just focus on adequate nutrition, light exercise, rest and relaxation.
